lesson.title: JSON: A Text Format That Speaks Python's Own Language
lesson.summary: JSON is a text-based data format built out of the same shapes as Python dictionaries and lists, and the json module converts directly between JSON text and those familiar Python objects.
lesson.body:
CSV is great at one thing: flat tables of rows and columns. But a lot of real data is not flat. Think of a student record that has a name, a grade level, and also a list of courses, where the number of courses is different for every student. Cramming that into a CSV row is awkward. JSON, short for JavaScript Object Notation, was designed for exactly this kind of nested data, and despite the name it is not tied to JavaScript at all. It has become a language-independent standard used by web APIs, configuration files, and countless programs, precisely because its two basic containers map so directly onto structures you already know from Python: a JSON object, written with curly braces and key/value pairs, looks and behaves like a Python dictionary, and a JSON array, written with square brackets, looks and behaves like a Python list.

Python's json module reads and writes this format. To work with an actual file on disk, you use json.dump() to write a Python object out as JSON text, and json.load() to read JSON text back in as a Python object. Both function names end in the same place the file-writing and file-reading methods you already know operate, on an open file object.

```python
import json

student = {
    "name": "Priya",
    "grade": 11,
    "courses": ["AP CS", "Calculus", "Chemistry"],
    "honor_roll": True
}

with open("student.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(student, f, indent=2)

with open("student.json", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)

print(loaded["name"])
print(loaded["courses"])
print(loaded == student)
```

This prints:

```
Priya
['AP CS', 'Calculus', 'Chemistry']
True
```

The last line is the important one: loaded is a completely new dictionary, built fresh by reading the file, and yet it is equal to the original student dictionary in every detail, because the trip through JSON preserved the structure exactly. The indent=2 argument to json.dump() is optional. It tells the json module to spread the output across multiple lines with two spaces of indentation per nesting level, purely to make the resulting file readable to a human. Leave indent out and you get the same data packed onto one dense line, which is smaller but harder to read.

Sometimes you have JSON as a string already in memory, perhaps received from a web request, rather than sitting in a file. For that case the json module has string equivalents: json.dumps() (with an s, for "dump string") converts a Python object into a JSON string instead of writing it to a file, and json.loads() converts a JSON string back into a Python object. The logic is identical to dump() and load(); only the source and destination change, from a file to a plain string.

The next chapter looks more closely at exactly which Python types correspond to which JSON types, because the correspondence is close but not perfect, and knowing where it breaks down will save you from some confusing bugs.
